Q: Disable Visual Studio 2022 Sign In prompt? A:

Wanted to say thank you to Sollace for the solution, it does seem to work. But there is something else worth mentioning since my path did not line up with any of the other posts here. For me, the path to the file was here:

C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Community\Common7\ServiceHub\Hosts\ServiceHub.Host.netfx.x86\ServiceHub.IdentityHost.exe

Not only that, the file also exists in two other places. But renaming these causes Visual Studio 2022 to crash shortly after opening a project file. So do NOT rename the file in these locations. I imagine if you have other versions of .NET SDK installed, there could end up being even more locations.

C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Community\Common7\ServiceHub\Hosts\ServiceHub.Host.dotnet.x64\net8.0-windows8.0\ServiceHub.IdentityHost.exe

C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Community\Common7\ServiceHub\Hosts\ServiceHub.Host.dotnet.x64\net10.0-windows10.0.19041.0\ServiceHub.IdentityHost.exe

Q: Attempt at SSIS Execution Throws Invalid object name 'SSISDB.catalog.customized_logging_levels' A:

This worked for me.

  1. Create the SSISDB Catalog on 2017.

  2. Once the SSISDB database is created automatically.

  3. Script the missing objects from the SQL Version 2017. Table - SSISDB.internal.customized_logging_levels View - SSISDB.catalog.customized_logging_levels Stored procedures - set_customized_logging_level_value set_customized_logging_level_description rename_customized_logging_level delete_customized_logging_level create_customized_logging_level

  4. Restore the SSISDB database from the backup of SQL Server 2014.

  5. Change the SSISDB database owner sa.

  6. Create the above scripted objects.

Q: How to start Outlook from within a batch file on Windows XP A:

I actually didn't realize I could create a task using the Task Scheduler program. Doing as you suggested and providing my Windows password for the task works perfectly. I was adding the task via the command line:

at 3:00 /every:s d:\batfiles\Start_Outlook.bat

So as expected in Task Scheduler this was shown as been created by the System user. I'm still curious if anyone has a method that would work to start Outlook via a batch file that is run by the System user.

Q: What is difference between foreign key and reference key? A:

There are 2 ways to declare a foreign key(s):

  1. if the foreign key is a SINGLE attribute:

    REFERENCES <Table> (<attribute>)

  2. if foreign keys are a LIST of attributes

    FOREIGN KEY (<attributes>) REFERENCES <table>

Q: How to access to Outlook (desktop client on macOS) stored emails programmatically A:

I know this is an old question, but I've gone and reverse engineered the format properly, so here's an actual answer.

Short version: it's not encrypted, it's LZ4-compressed inside a checksummed block container. The strange characters you're seeing are back-references, not corruption.

Look at your own sample:

<meta http-equiv="Content-Type" cp="text/;ñ; charset=utf-8">

That should read content="text/html; charset=utf-8". The cp= is what's left after the compressor replaced ontent-Ty with a 2-byte back-reference pointing at the earlier Content-Type string. Same reason you see runs of plaintext with occasional bytes missing mid-word. The literals are stored as-is, which is why grep finds readable text, but you can't just read the file linearly.

The file itself:

  • First 8 bytes are ASCII Nostromo, then a version byte

  • The rest is a series of blocks, each with a 40-byte header carrying two CRC-32s (zlib polynomial), a magic 0x5d0245643b706a05, the compressed length, and the exact inflated length

  • The payload is standard LZ4 block format

  • Inside a decompressed block, messages are anchored on the UTF-16LE string IPM.Note, with the sender, subject and preview as NUL-terminated UTF-16LE runs around it

The two CRCs are what makes this tractable. You scan for the magic, verify both checksums, then decompress and require the output to hit the declared length exactly. A wrong offset fails on all three, so you never get the plausible-but-wrong output you'd get from carving blindly. I got 99.9% of blocks on a 56 MB store that way.

Two things worth knowing before you start:

Outlook rewrites the file while it's running (it holds HxStore.lock). I watched one shrink mid-session. Work on a copy.

The store is a cache, not an archive. It keeps the full body for a minority of messages and a ~255 character preview for the rest, fetching the real body from the server when you open the message. If your bodies look truncated, that's the format, not your decoder.

On Windows: the same Hx engine backs Windows Mail and I'd expect new Outlook on Windows too. HxCore carries NostromoH, NostromoH9 and NostromoI as literals, and the Boncaldo post you linked shows `'h'` on Windows against `'i'` on macOS, so the container should be identical. I've only tested macOS though, so I'd treat that as likely rather than confirmed. The tool accepts both version bytes and warns on anything else, and since every block is checksummed a real format difference would fail loudly rather than quietly giving you wrong data. If you do run it against a Windows store I'd be interested to hear how it goes.

Full write-up, including the bits I got wrong first (I spent a while looking for Windows FILETIME timestamps before working out they're .NET ticks with a year 1 epoch):

https://securized.dev/hxstore-reverse-engineering/

Format spec and a Rust parser that dumps the whole store into SQLite with FTS5 search:

https://github.com/securized/hxstore-reverse-engineering

Q: Python uv.lock and .gitignore A:

It depends

As with many things in configurable, version tracking (via git or otherwise) the configuration options exist because there will be exceptions. So it is difficult to answer definitively as which is better, but here is how one can approach a given case.

Arguments Against ignoring uv.lock

No, uv.lock should not be added to .gitignore, but on the contrary, committed to the Git repository, as recommended by uv:

This file should be checked into version control, allowing for consistent and reproducible installations across machines.

  • This use of lock files is not as trivial to modify, as write repository access will be needed; which happens to mitigate some supply-chain-poisoning risks; Bad-actors can't both poison dependencies and automatically leverage that against your repo, (not without also updating your uv.lock file to allow the poisoned version)

Arguments For ignoring uv.lock

  • as already mentioned by others; over zealous version pinning reduces portability, especially for binary packages.

Maintaining a complex/large set of dependencies with UV can still be done, there is less friction if the uv.lock file is omitted from the tracked files, as each developer can generate their own lockfile for their own environment (the lock file does not replace the dependancy configs, just pins dependencies to specific variant(s))

Unless you are confident in managing your lockfile meticulously, you may find it more maintainable to omit the uv.lock

  • Not everyone else will want to use uv
